questions.stem: Prosocial behaviour is best defined as:
options: behaviour that matches what the rest of a group does
voluntary behaviour intended to help or benefit others
behaviour that follows the rules set by an authority
behaviour that causes harm or distress to other people
questions.explanation: Prosocial behaviour is any voluntary action intended to benefit others, such as helping, sharing or comforting. It can be done for selfless or selfish reasons.

questions.stem: Altruism differs from other prosocial behaviour because it is:
options: helping that is done to gain public praise
helping with no expectation of any reward
helping that is required by law or rules
helping that is done only for family members
questions.explanation: Altruism is helping purely out of concern for another person, with no expectation of reward. Prosocial behaviour more broadly may be motivated by rewards, praise or obligation.

questions.stem: A student helps a classmate with homework because the classmate helped her last week. This is best explained by:
options: diffusion of responsibility
the frustration-aggression hypothesis
the norm of reciprocity
deindividuation
questions.explanation: The norm of reciprocity is the social expectation that we should help those who have helped us. It is a common motive for prosocial behaviour.

questions.stem: Antisocial behaviour is behaviour that:
options: involves going along with the opinions of a group
is shown only by people who have broken the law
causes harm, distress or hostility towards others
is intended to help or benefit another person
questions.explanation: Antisocial behaviour causes harm, distress, harassment or hostility and violates social rules or others' rights. It lies on a continuum from rudeness to serious crime, so not all of it is criminal.

questions.stem: A football player deliberately trips an opponent to stop a likely goal, with no anger towards him. This is:
options: altruism
reciprocity
instrumental aggression
hostile aggression
questions.explanation: Instrumental aggression is harm used as a means to achieve a goal. Hostile aggression is driven by anger, with harm as the main aim.

questions.stem: Which is an example of antisocial behaviour that is not necessarily criminal?
options: deliberately excluding and mocking a classmate
breaking into a house and stealing property
seriously assaulting a stranger in the street
selling illegal drugs to young people at school
questions.explanation: Excluding and mocking someone causes distress and is antisocial, but is not usually a crime. Burglary, assault and drug dealing are criminal behaviours.

questions.stem: Toddlers often help adults pick up dropped objects without being asked or rewarded. What does this suggest about prosocial behaviour?
options: It appears only in adults who have been rewarded for it
It is entirely inborn and is not affected by experience
It appears early, and then develops with socialisation
It is learned only once children start formal schooling
questions.explanation: Prosocial behaviour is evident in very young children, which suggests some inborn basis, but how and how often it is expressed changes with socialisation and experience.

questions.stem: The bystander effect is the finding that:
options: people are more likely to help when others are present
people help only those who are similar to themselves
people always help when they see an emergency happen
people are less likely to help when others are present
questions.explanation: The bystander effect is the tendency for individuals to be less likely to help in an emergency when other bystanders are present.

questions.stem: In Darley and Latane's (1968) study, participants heard another participant apparently having a seizure over an intercom. What did they find?
options: All participants helped at once, whatever the size of the group
No participants helped, because the seizure seemed so unrealistic
Participants who thought others could hear were less likely to help
Participants helped more often when they thought many others could hear
questions.explanation: Participants who believed they were the only listener were much more likely to help, and to help quickly, than those who believed four others could also hear. This shows diffusion of responsibility.

questions.stem: Diffusion of responsibility means that in a group:
options: people copy whatever the most popular member does
each person feels less personal responsibility to act
each person feels a greater duty to help than alone
the leader of the group always takes the responsibility
questions.explanation: When many people are present, responsibility for helping is spread among them, so each person feels less obliged to act and assumes someone else will.

questions.stem: Participants fill in a form while smoke pours into the room. Alone, most report it; with two calm confederates who ignore it, few do. Which process best explains the difference?
options: Participants were deindividuated because they were anonymous in a crowd
Participants were frustrated by the smoke, so they acted aggressively
Others' calm behaviour led participants to judge it was not an emergency
Participants felt more personally responsible when others were present
questions.explanation: When others appear unconcerned, people look to them to interpret an ambiguous situation and conclude there is no emergency. This is called pluralistic ignorance or social influence.

questions.stem: According to Latane and Darley's decision model, which step must come first before a bystander helps?
options: noticing that something is happening
deciding how to help the person
assuming personal responsibility
interpreting it as an emergency
questions.explanation: The model's steps are: notice the event, interpret it as an emergency, assume responsibility, decide how to help, and then act. Failure at any step means no help.

questions.stem: Piliavin and colleagues (1969) staged collapses on a New York subway train. A victim carrying a cane was helped more often than a victim who appeared drunk. How does a cost-benefit view explain this?
options: Helping the drunk victim seemed more costly, such as being unpleasant or risky
Helping the cane victim seemed more costly, so more people chose to help
The drunk victim was surrounded by more people, causing diffusion of responsibility
The cane victim was in a laboratory, so the situation seemed less real
questions.explanation: In a cost-benefit (cost-reward) analysis, bystanders weigh the costs of helping against the costs of not helping. Helping a drunk person may seem more unpleasant or risky, so they were helped less.

questions.stem: Unlike in laboratory studies, Piliavin found that the number of bystanders on the train did not reduce helping. Which is a likely reason?
options: Subway passengers had all been told the true aim of the study
The passengers had been randomly selected from a list of volunteers
The passengers were anonymous, so deindividuation increased helping
The victim was clearly visible and the emergency was not ambiguous
questions.explanation: On the train, bystanders could see the victim directly and could not leave, so the emergency was unambiguous and hard to ignore. In the intercom study, participants could not see the victim or the other listeners.

questions.stem: Which situational factor makes a bystander more likely to help?
options: being the only person present who can help
being in a great hurry to get to an appointment
being surrounded by many calm, unconcerned people
being unsure whether there is really an emergency
questions.explanation: Being alone removes diffusion of responsibility, so the bystander feels fully responsible. Time pressure, unconcerned others and ambiguity all reduce helping.

questions.stem: Batson's empathy-altruism hypothesis proposes that:
options: people help mainly because they are told to by an authority
feeling empathy for someone leads to truly altruistic helping
people help only when the rewards outweigh the costs to them
people help in order to relieve their own feelings of distress
questions.explanation: Batson argued that empathic concern, feeling for another person's situation, produces genuine altruistic motivation to help, even when helping is costly and escape is easy.

questions.stem: In Batson's research, participants who felt high empathy for a person receiving shocks offered to take her place even when they could easily leave. Why does this support the empathy-altruism hypothesis?
options: It shows that empathy has no effect on helping when costs are low
If helping were only to relieve their own distress, they would have simply left
If helping were altruistic, they would have chosen to leave the study instead
It shows that people help only when others are watching and judging them
questions.explanation: Leaving would have ended the participants' own discomfort, so choosing to help instead suggests their motive was concern for the victim, not self-interest.

questions.stem: Students training to become ministers were sent to give a talk. On the way, they passed a man slumped in a doorway. Those told they were late were much less likely to help. This shows the influence of:
options: situational factors on helping
personality traits on helping
reciprocity on helping
deindividuation on helping
questions.explanation: Even people who might be expected to be very helpful helped less when under time pressure. This shows how strongly situational factors affect prosocial behaviour.

questions.stem: The frustration-aggression hypothesis (Dollard, Miller and colleagues, 1939) originally proposed that:
options: frustration only occurs in people who are aggressive
frustration always leads to some form of aggression
aggression is learned by watching aggressive models
aggression is reduced when people feel empathy
questions.explanation: Frustration is the feeling of being blocked from a goal. The original hypothesis claimed frustration always produces aggression and aggression always comes from frustration.

questions.stem: A student who is denied a promotion at work goes home and yells at his younger sister. In frustration-aggression terms, this is:
options: altruism
reciprocity
displaced aggression
instrumental aggression
questions.explanation: When aggression cannot safely be directed at the source of frustration, it may be displaced onto a safer target. The boss is a risky target, so the sister receives it.

questions.stem: Berkowitz revised the frustration-aggression hypothesis. Which statement reflects his revision?
options: Frustration creates readiness for aggression, which cues such as weapons can trigger
Frustration never leads to aggression unless a person is rewarded for it
Aggression is caused only by inherited traits and never by frustration
Frustration always leads to aggression in every person and situation
questions.explanation: Berkowitz argued that frustration produces anger and a readiness to aggress, but aggression is more likely when cues associated with aggression, such as weapons, are present. Frustration does not always lead to aggression.

questions.stem: Which observation challenges the original frustration-aggression hypothesis?
options: Aggression is often directed at targets who did not cause the frustration
Frustration from heat and crowding is linked with more aggressive acts
Some frustrated people respond by withdrawing or by solving the problem
Some people act aggressively after being blocked from reaching a goal
questions.explanation: If frustration always caused aggression, withdrawal or problem solving would not occur. The other observations are consistent with the hypothesis.

questions.stem: Conformity is:
options: changing behaviour or beliefs to match a group
following a direct order from an authority figure
helping others without expecting anything back
behaving aggressively towards members of a group
questions.explanation: Conformity is adjusting one's behaviour or beliefs to fit group norms. Obedience is following direct orders from an authority figure.

questions.stem: In Asch's line experiment, participants judged which of three lines matched a target line after several confederates gave the same wrong answer. What did he find?
options: Every participant conformed on every trial that was in the study
Participants conformed only when the confederates were their friends
Many participants conformed to the wrong answer on at least one trial
No participants conformed because the right answer was obvious
questions.explanation: About three-quarters of participants conformed at least once, and about a third of responses on the critical trials conformed, even though the correct answer was clear.

questions.stem: In a variation of Asch's study, one confederate gave the correct answer before the participant responded. What happened to conformity, and why?
options: It rose sharply, because the participant wanted to please the ally
It did not change, because group size is the only factor involved
It disappeared entirely, because all pressure from the group ended
It dropped sharply, because the group was no longer unanimous
questions.explanation: Having just one ally broke the group's unanimity and greatly reduced conformity. Unanimity is a key factor in conformity.

questions.stem: In Zimbardo's Stanford Prison Experiment (1971), students randomly assigned to be guards soon treated 'prisoners' harshly. What does this suggest?
options: Social roles and situations can strongly shape behaviour
Only people with aggressive personalities become guards
Random assignment makes behaviour impossible to predict
Prisoners are naturally more obedient than other people
questions.explanation: Because the students were randomly assigned and screened for psychological problems, the guards' harshness was attributed to the power of the role and situation.

questions.stem: Why was the Stanford Prison Experiment stopped after six days instead of the planned two weeks?
options: The data had already proved the hypothesis
Participants were suffering distress and harm
The researchers ran out of funding for the study
The guards refused to take part any longer
questions.explanation: Prisoners showed serious emotional distress and guards' behaviour became abusive. The study is widely criticised for failing to protect participants, and Zimbardo's dual role as researcher and superintendent.

questions.stem: Deindividuation is a state in which people in a group:
options: follow the orders of a leader because they respect authority
lose self-awareness and feel less responsible for their actions
become more aware of their own values and personal standards
feel strongly obliged to help any victim they see in trouble
questions.explanation: Deindividuation occurs when anonymity and group immersion reduce self-awareness and personal responsibility, which can lead to behaviour people would not show alone.

questions.stem: Online, people posting anonymously make more hostile comments than when posting under their real names. This is best explained by:
options: conformity to a majority
deindividuation
reciprocity
empathy
questions.explanation: Anonymity reduces self-awareness and fear of being identified, which is deindividuation. This lowers restraint against antisocial behaviour.

questions.stem: In Milgram's obedience study, most participants continued giving what they believed were dangerous electric shocks when told to by the experimenter. This shows the power of:
options: obedience to authority
conformity to peers
altruism towards strangers
reciprocity between equals
questions.explanation: Obedience is following orders from a perceived authority. Participants obeyed the experimenter even though they believed they were harming someone.

questions.stem: Which is an individual factor rather than a situational factor affecting helping?
options: whether a person is in a hurry
a person's level of empathy
the number of bystanders
how ambiguous the event is
questions.explanation: Individual factors are characteristics of the person, such as empathy, mood and skills. The number of bystanders, ambiguity and time pressure are features of the situation.

questions.stem: Children who often see family members helping neighbours tend to help others more themselves. This is best explained by:
options: socialisation through observing models
a fixed inherited level of helping
deindividuation in the family group
frustration from blocked goals
questions.explanation: Through socialisation, children learn prosocial behaviour by observing and imitating models and being praised for helping.

questions.stem: Twin studies suggest that empathy and helpfulness are partly heritable. Which conclusion is most accurate?
options: Socialisation has no effect on how helpful a person becomes
Situational factors have no effect once heredity is known
Both heredity and socialisation influence prosocial behaviour
Prosocial behaviour is entirely determined by a person's genes
questions.explanation: Genetic influences on empathy combine with socialisation and situational factors. No single factor fully determines whether a person helps.

questions.stem: According to a cost-benefit (cost-reward) analysis of helping, a bystander is most likely to help when:
options: many other bystanders are present and nobody else has yet helped
the victim is a stranger and the situation is very ambiguous
the costs of helping are low and the costs of not helping are high
the costs of helping are high and the rewards of helping are low
questions.explanation: Cost-benefit explanations say bystanders weigh the costs of helping (danger, effort, embarrassment) against the costs of not helping (guilt, blame). Helping is most likely when helping is cheap and not helping would feel costly.

questions.stem: A celebrity donates to a hospital appeal only when television cameras are present. Why is this prosocial but not altruistic?
options: It is done in a group rather than by one person alone
It involves money rather than time, effort or skills
It helps others but is motivated by expected reward
It harms others while appearing to be helpful to them
questions.explanation: Prosocial behaviour is any voluntary action that benefits others, whatever the motive. Altruism requires no expectation of reward, and helping in order to gain publicity is a selfish motive.

questions.stem: Which is an example of prosocial behaviour?
options: spreading a rumour to damage a classmate's name
refusing to follow a teacher's reasonable request
copying a friend's answers during a class test
comforting a friend who is upset after a loss
questions.explanation: Prosocial behaviour includes helping, sharing, comforting, cooperating and volunteering. Spreading rumours is relational aggression, a type of antisocial behaviour.

questions.stem: A school notices that a Year 3 student often defies teachers, bullies others and lies. Why do psychologists recommend acting early?
options: Antisocial behaviour in children always disappears without help by adolescence
Early antisocial behaviour is caused only by genes, so it cannot be changed later
Children under ten cannot show antisocial behaviour, so it must be a medical illness
Antisocial patterns seen early can escalate into chronic problems if unchecked
questions.explanation: Antisocial behaviour lies on a continuum and is often a coercive pattern that can be identified early. If unchecked it may escalate into a chronic behavioural disorder or criminal behaviour, so early intervention is recommended.
